title: The Angular Momentum Spiral
topics: ladder operators and the spectrum j(j+1)

sources.where: Q1 angular momentum and uncertainty, Q2 so(4)

intro: Rotations are the first symmetry the course takes seriously. Everything in this room follows from one line, $[L_i,L_j]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k$: it fixes the spectrum $j(j+1)$, the ladder matrix elements, the Pauli matrices, the uncertainty relations and, through $[H,\vec L]=0$, the degeneracy of every central-force problem. Three recent exam problems (FS26 Q1, FS22 Q2, FS26 Q3) are exactly these moves.

tutorial.title: The cones
tutorial.html: For $\ell=2$ the vector $\vec L$ has length $\hbar\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}=\hbar\sqrt6$ and $L_z\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\hbar$. Each glowing arrow sits on a cone of fixed $L_z$ and precesses: $L_x,L_y$ are completely undetermined, only $L_z$ and $\vec L^2$ are sharp.

tutorial.title: The ring of rungs
tutorial.html: The horizontal rungs are the five values of $L_z$. The ladder operators $L_\pm$ move the state one rung up or down; the top rung $m=\ell$ is the only one where $\Delta L_x\Delta L_y$ saturates the Heisenberg bound.

tutorial.title: Consoles
tutorial.html: Library: algebra, spin-1/2, spin-1 measurements, vector operators. Quiz: exam-style multiple choice. Derivation desk: proofs from the sheets and exams. Fights: step-by-step calculations. Boss gate: FS26 Q1, FS22 Q2, FS26 Q3.

encounters.title: The su(2) algebra, ladder operators and the spectrum j(j+1)

blocks.html: With $L_j=\varepsilon_{jkl}x_kp_l$ and $[x_k,p_l]=i\hbar\delta_{kl}$ one finds $[L_1,L_2]=[x_2p_3-x_3p_2,\,x_3p_1-x_1p_3]=i\hbar(x_1p_2-x_2p_1)=i\hbar L_3$, and cyclicity of the indices gives the rest. The script uses dimensionless generators $M_i=L_i/\hbar$ ($[M_1,M_2]=iM_3$); exams use $L_i$ with $\hbar$.
Ladder operators. $L_\pm=L_1\pm iL_2$ satisfy

If $L_3|m\rangle=\hbar m|m\rangle$, then $L_\pm|m\rangle$ has eigenvalue $\hbar(m\pm1)$: the operators climb the ladder. A finite representation needs a top state $L_+|j,j\rangle=0$. Then $\vec L^2=\hbar^2j(j+1)$ on the whole multiplet, and the norms $\|L_\pm|j,m\rangle\|^2=\langle L_\mp L_\pm\rangle=\hbar^2[j(j+1)-m(m\pm1)]$ must be non-negative, so the chain must also end at the bottom, $m=-j$. Going from $j$ down to $-j$ takes an integer number $2j$ of steps:

blocks.label: script (7.37)-(7.51); the exam hint prints exactly this

blocks.html: For $j=1$ in the basis $|1,1\rangle,|1,0\rangle,|1,-1\rangle$: $L_3=\hbar\,\mathrm{diag}(1,0,-1)$, $L_1=\frac{L_++L_-}2=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $L_2=\frac{L_+-L_-}{2i}=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}0&-i&0\\i&0&-i\\0&i&0\end{pmatrix}$.
Orbital angular momentum only realises integer $j=\ell$ (single-valued wave functions $Y_{\ell m}$). Half-integer $j$ are genuine representations of the covering group $SU(2)$: that is spin.

$\vec L^{\,2}=\hbar^2j(j+1)$, not $\hbar^2j^2$: the vector never points exactly along $z$ because $L_x,L_y$ cannot vanish simultaneously with $L_z$. Also $L_\pm$ are not Hermitian, so $L_\pm|m\rangle$ is not normalised without the square root.
FS26 Q1(i) (5 pt) and FS22 Q2(i)-(ii) (4 pt): derive $[L_j,L_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}L_l$ via $[L_1,L_2]$ and cyclicity, and compute $[L_3,L_\pm]$, $[L_+,L_-]$.

blocks.html: For $j=\frac12$ the generators are $S_i=\frac\hbar2\sigma_i$ with the Pauli matrices

blocks.html: A rotation by $2\pi$ gives $U=-1$: a spinor changes sign. $\tilde x=\vec x\cdot\vec\sigma\mapsto U\tilde xU^\dagger$ is a rotation of $\vec x$ ($\det\tilde x=-\vec x^2$ is preserved), and $U$ and $-U$ give the same rotation: $SU(2)\to SO(3)$ is 2-to-1 with kernel $\{\pm1\}$.
State from a direction. If $\langle\vec\sigma\rangle=\vec e$ with polar angles $\theta,\varphi$ then $\chi$ is the $+1$ eigenvector of $\vec e\cdot\vec\sigma$ (sheet 11 Q2):
The half angle is the whole story: the spinor rotates at half the speed of the vector, which is why $\theta=\pi$ (a flip) sends $\cos\frac\theta2$ to $0$ and why a $2\pi$ rotation is only $-1$.

Do not write $e^{-i\omega\sigma_3}$; with $S=\frac\hbar2\sigma$ the angle is divided by two. Do not conclude that $-1$ is unobservable in general: it is a global phase for one state but a relative phase between a spinor and a spin-0 partner.
FS24 Q3(b): "rotate the spin, then measure $z$" equals "measure the unrotated spin along the rotated axis". Sheet 11 Q2 asks for exactly the spinor above.

encounters.title: Spin 1: measurement, expectation values and uncertainties

blocks.html: This is the FS26 Q1 recipe. A measurement of an observable with result $\lambda$ projects onto the eigenspace of $\lambda$, so the post-measurement state is the eigenvector. For $L_1=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$ the eigenvalue $\hbar$ gives (solve $\frac1{\sqrt2}(b)=a$, $\frac1{\sqrt2}(a+c)=b$):

Trick (iv). For an eigenvector $L_1|\psi\rangle=\hbar|\psi\rangle$: $\langle\psi|[L_1,O]|\psi\rangle=\hbar\langle O\rangle-\hbar\langle O\rangle=0$ for any $O$. With $O=L_3$: $\hbar\langle[L_1,L_3]\rangle=-i\hbar\,\hbar\langle L_2\rangle=0$. With $O=L_2L_3+L_3L_2$ one gets $\langle L_2^2\rangle=\langle L_3^2\rangle$. Since $\vec L^2=2\hbar^2$ and $\langle L_1^2\rangle=\hbar^2$:

blocks.tex: \langle L_2^2\rangle=\langle L_3^2\rangle=\tfrac{\hbar^2}2,\quad \Delta L_1=0,\ \ \Delta L_2=\Delta L_3=\tfrac\hbar{\sqrt2},\quad \Delta L_2\Delta L_3=\tfrac{\hbar^2}2=\tfrac\hbar2|\langle L_1\rangle|
blocks.label: FS26 Q1(iv)-(v): the bound is saturated

blocks.html: General $|l,m\rangle$ (FS22 Q2). $\langle L_1\rangle=\langle L_2\rangle=0$ because $L_1,L_2$ are combinations of $L_\pm$ which change $m$. Since $|l,m\rangle$ is an eigenstate of $L_3$, $\langle[L_3,A]\rangle=0$ for all $A$; choosing $A=L_1L_2+L_2L_1$ and using $[L_3,A]=2i\hbar(L_2^2-L_1^2)$ gives $\langle L_1^2\rangle=\langle L_2^2\rangle$, and with $\langle\vec L^2\rangle=\hbar^2l(l+1)$:
The inequality holds because $l(l+1)-m^2\ge l(l+1)-l^2=l\ge|m|$, with equality only for $|m|=l$ (and $l\ge1$ to be non-trivial).

In $|l,m\rangle$ the vector sits on a cone around $z$: $L_z=\hbar m$ is sharp, $L_x^2+L_y^2=\hbar^2[l(l+1)-m^2]$ is sharp, but the azimuth is completely unknown. The uncertainty is large because $L_x,L_y$ cannot be sharp when $L_z$ is.

$\Delta L_2\Delta L_3\ge\frac\hbar2|\langle L_1\rangle|$ is the relevant bound for that pair; the other combinations in FS26 Q1(v) give $0\ge\frac\hbar2|\langle L_2\rangle|=0$ and are trivially satisfied because $\Delta L_1=0$. Do not claim $0\ge\hbar^2/2$.
FS26 Q1 (20 pt) and FS22 Q2 (15 pt) are the same computation twice: expectation values by selection rule, variances by symmetry, bound by one line.

blocks.html: The generators act on operators by commutation: an operator triple $\vec J$ is a vector operator iff

blocks.label: sheet 12 Q2; holds for x, p, L

blocks.html: This is the adjoint action, the representation $D^1$, so $\vec J\cdot\vec K$ is a scalar ($[L_i,\vec J\cdot\vec K]=0$) and the symmetric traceless products form a $D^2$ (five components); $D^1\otimes D^1=D^0\oplus D^1\oplus D^2$.

Rotational symmetry (FS26 Q3). With $H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2+V$ and $L_j=-i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}x_k\partial_l$: the kinetic term commutes since $[\nabla^2,x_k\partial_l]=2\partial_k\partial_l$, which is symmetric and vanishes against $\varepsilon_{jkl}$. The potential term gives

Consequences: $H,\vec L^2,L_3$ commute, so eigenstates can be chosen as $\psi=R(r)Y_{\ell m}$ and each level is at least $(2\ell+1)$-fold degenerate: $L_\pm$ commute with $H$ and move within the multiplet.

The oscillator triplet. For $V=\frac12m\omega^2\vec x^2$ the functions $\psi_i=x_ie^{-m\omega\vec x^2/2\hbar}$ are eigenfunctions with $E=\frac52\hbar\omega$, and $L_j\psi_k=-i\hbar\varepsilon_{jak}\psi_a$ (the Gaussian is rotation invariant, so only $x_k$ is rotated). Hence $L_3\psi_1=i\hbar\psi_2$, $L_3\psi_2=-i\hbar\psi_1$, $L_3\psi_3=0$:
The Cartesian functions $x_i$ and the spherical $Y_{1m}\propto x\pm iy,\ z$ are two bases of the same three-dimensional $D^1$: that is what "$\vec x$ is a vector" means.

$[H,L_j]=0$ does not mean "$V$ is spherical" only: it means $V$ depends on $r$ alone. A potential like $V=V(r)+\vec c\cdot\vec x$ breaks the symmetry; FS22 Q3(iii) conserves only $L\cdot k$ and $p_z$ in a similar way.

encounters.title: $[L_i,L_j]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k$ and $[L_3,\vec L^2]=0$

source.where: Question 1 (i), 5 pt; also FS22 Q2(i) and sheet 8 Q1(i)

encounters.goal: Show $[L_1,L_2]=i\hbar L_3$ for $L_j=\varepsilon_{jkl}x_kp_l$, extend to all indices and prove $[L_3,\vec L^{\,2}]=0$.

steps.prompt: Expand $[L_1,L_2]$ into four commutators and say which are non-zero.
steps.reveal: $[x_2p_3-x_3p_2,\ x_3p_1-x_1p_3]=[x_2p_3,x_3p_1]-[x_2p_3,x_1p_3]-[x_3p_2,x_3p_1]+[x_3p_2,x_1p_3]$. Terms 2 and 3 vanish: $x_2p_3$ and $x_1p_3$ have no conjugate pair.

steps.prompt: Evaluate the two surviving terms with $[AB,C]=A[B,C]+[A,C]B$.
steps.reveal: $[x_2p_3,x_3p_1]=x_2[p_3,x_3]p_1=-i\hbar x_2p_1$ and $[x_3p_2,x_1p_3]=p_2[x_3,p_3]x_1=i\hbar x_1p_2$ (everything else commutes).

steps.prompt: Add and recognise $L_3$; then argue for the other pairs.
steps.reveal: $[L_1,L_2]=i\hbar(x_1p_2-x_2p_1)=i\hbar L_3$. The definition $L_j=\varepsilon_{jkl}x_kp_l$ is invariant under cyclic permutations $1\to2\to3\to1$, so $[L_2,L_3]=i\hbar L_1$, $[L_3,L_1]=i\hbar L_2$; antisymmetry gives the rest: $[L_j,L_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}L_l$.

$[L_3,L_1^2]=[L_3,L_1]L_1+L_1[L_3,L_1]=i\hbar(L_2L_1+L_1L_2)$ and $[L_3,L_2^2]=[L_3,L_2]L_2+L_2[L_3,L_2]=-i\hbar(L_1L_2+L_2L_1)$. The sum is $0$, and $[L_3,L_3^2]=0$, so $[L_3,\vec L^2]=0$; by cyclicity all $L_j$ commute with $\vec L^2$.

keyPoints: cyclic permutation of indices gives all other commutators
$[L_3,L_1^2+L_2^2]=0$ because the two terms cancel, hence $\vec L^2$ is a Casimir

encounters.title: Ladder spectrum: $\vec L^2=\hbar^2j(j+1)$ and $L_\pm|j,m\rangle$

source.where: Ch. 7.4, eqs. (7.37)-(7.51); FS22 Q2(ii)-(iii) and FS26 Q1 hint

encounters.goal: From $[L_3,L_\pm]=\pm\hbar L_\pm$ and $[L_+,L_-]=2\hbar L_3$ derive $\vec L^2=\hbar^2j(j+1)$, $j\in\frac12\mathbb N_0$, and $L_\pm|j,m\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m\pm1)}|j,m\pm1\rangle$.

steps.prompt: Show that $L_\pm$ shift $m$ by $\pm1$ and commute with $\vec L^2$.
steps.reveal: $L_3L_\pm|m\rangle=(L_\pm L_3\pm\hbar L_\pm)|m\rangle=\hbar(m\pm1)L_\pm|m\rangle$. $[\vec L^2,L_\pm]=0$ because $\vec L^2$ commutes with every $L_j$ (previous derivation).

steps.prompt: The top state obeys $L_+|j,j\rangle=0$. Find the eigenvalue of $\vec L^2$.
steps.reveal: $\vec L^2|j,j\rangle=(L_-L_++L_3^2+\hbar L_3)|j,j\rangle=\hbar^2(j^2+j)|j,j\rangle$; since $\vec L^2$ is the same on the whole multiplet, $\vec L^2=\hbar^2j(j+1)$.

steps.prompt: Compute the norm of $L_\pm|j,m\rangle$, giving the matrix elements.
steps.reveal: $\|L_+|m\rangle\|^2=\langle L_-L_+\rangle=\hbar^2[j(j+1)-m^2-m]=\hbar^2[j(j+1)-m(m+1)]$, similarly $\|L_-|m\rangle\|^2=\hbar^2[j(j+1)-m(m-1)]$; fixing the phase to be real gives the formula.
Lowering from $m=j$ must stop: $L_-|j,-j'\rangle=0$ needs $j(j+1)=(-j')(-j'-1)=j'(j'+1)$, so $j'=j$. The chain $j,j-1,\dots,-j$ has $2j$ steps, hence $2j\in\mathbb N_0$ and $\dim=2j+1$.

keyPoints: positive norms give the $\sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m\pm1)}$ and force the chain to end at $-j$, so $2j\in\mathbb N_0$

encounters.title: Spin-1/2 rotation formula $e^{-i\omega\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$ and the $2\pi$ sign

source.where: Ch. 7.5-7.6, eq. (7.60); sheet 9 Q3; sheet 11 Q2

encounters.goal: Show $\sigma_j\sigma_k=\delta_{jk}+i\varepsilon_{jkl}\sigma_l$, derive $U(\omega\vec n)=\cos\frac\omega2-i\sin\frac\omega2\,\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma$ and the kernel $\{\pm1\}$ of $SU(2)\to SO(3)$.

steps.reveal: $\sigma_1\sigma_2=i\sigma_3=-\sigma_2\sigma_1$; with $\sigma_j^2=1$: $\sigma_j\sigma_k=\delta_{jk}+i\varepsilon_{jkl}\sigma_l$. Hence $(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec a)(\vec\sigma\cdot\vec b)=\vec a\cdot\vec b+i\vec\sigma\cdot(\vec a\wedge\vec b)$.

steps.prompt: Compute $(\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma)^2$ for a unit vector.
steps.reveal: $\vec n\cdot\vec n+i\vec\sigma\cdot(\vec n\wedge\vec n)=1$.

steps.prompt: Sum the exponential series of $e^{-i(\omega/2)\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma}$.
steps.reveal: Even powers give $(\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma)^{2k}=1$: $\sum\frac{(-1)^k(\omega/2)^{2k}}{(2k)!}=\cos\frac\omega2$. Odd powers give $\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma$ times $-i\sum\frac{(-1)^k(\omega/2)^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}=-i\sin\frac\omega2$. So $U=\cos\frac\omega2-i\sin\frac\omega2\,\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma$.

$U(2\pi\vec n)=-1$ for every axis. The rotation $\tilde x\mapsto U\tilde xU^\dagger$ is unchanged by $U\to-U$, so $\pm U$ give the same $R\in SO(3)$: the map is 2-to-1 with kernel $\{\pm1\}$ and $SU(2)/\{\pm1\}\cong SO(3)$.

encounters.title: $\Delta L_1\Delta L_2=\frac{\hbar^2}2[l(l+1)-m^2]$ and the Heisenberg bound
encounters.goal: In $|l,m\rangle$ show $\langle L_1\rangle=\langle L_2\rangle=0$, $\Delta L_1\Delta L_2=\frac{\hbar^2}2[l(l+1)-m^2]$, and that this respects $\Delta L_1\Delta L_2\ge\frac\hbar2|\langle L_3\rangle|$.

steps.reveal: $L_1=\frac12(L_++L_-)$ and $L_2=\frac1{2i}(L_+-L_-)$ map $|l,m\rangle$ to $|l,m\pm1\rangle\perp|l,m\rangle$, so both expectation values vanish.

$[L_3,L_1L_2+L_2L_1]=i\hbar(L_2L_2-L_1L_1)+i\hbar(L_2L_2-L_1L_1)=2i\hbar(L_2^2-L_1^2)$ and $\langle[L_3,A]\rangle=\hbar m\langle A\rangle-\hbar m\langle A\rangle=0$, hence $\langle L_1^2\rangle=\langle L_2^2\rangle$.

$\langle L_1^2+L_2^2\rangle=\hbar^2[l(l+1)-m^2]$, so $\langle L_1^2\rangle=\langle L_2^2\rangle=\frac{\hbar^2}2[l(l+1)-m^2]$. With vanishing means, $\Delta L_1=\Delta L_2=\hbar\sqrt{\tfrac12[l(l+1)-m^2]}$ and $\Delta L_1\Delta L_2=\frac{\hbar^2}2[l(l+1)-m^2]$.

steps.prompt: State the uncertainty relation and compare.
steps.reveal: $\Delta A\Delta B\ge\frac12|\langle[A,B]\rangle|$ gives $\Delta L_1\Delta L_2\ge\frac12|\langle i\hbar L_3\rangle|=\frac{\hbar^2|m|}2$. Since $l(l+1)-m^2\ge l(l+1)-l^2=l\ge|m|$, (7) is compatible, with equality iff $|m|=l$.

encounters.title: Spinor from $\langle\vec\sigma\rangle=\vec e$ (sheet 11 Q2)
encounters.goal: Show that a spin-1/2 state with $\langle\vec\sigma\rangle=\vec e=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$ is $\chi=(\cos\frac\theta2,e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac\theta2)^T$ and compute $P(S_z=+\hbar/2)$.

steps.prompt: Argue that $\langle\vec\sigma\rangle=\vec e$ with $|\vec e|=1$ means $\chi$ is an eigenvector of $\vec e\cdot\vec\sigma$.
steps.reveal: $\langle\vec e\cdot\vec\sigma\rangle=|\vec e|^2=1$ and the eigenvalues of $\vec e\cdot\vec\sigma$ are $\pm1$ (it squares to $1$), so $\chi$ must lie in the $+1$ eigenspace.
First row: $a\cos\theta+b\sin\theta e^{-i\varphi}=a\Rightarrow b=a\,e^{i\varphi}\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=a\,e^{i\varphi}\tan\frac\theta2$.

steps.prompt: Normalise and read off the probability.
steps.reveal: $|a|^2(1+\tan^2\frac\theta2)=1\Rightarrow a=\cos\frac\theta2$, $b=e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac\theta2$ (global phase free). $P(S_z=+\hbar/2)=|a|^2=\cos^2\frac\theta2=\frac{1+e_3}2$.

keyPoints: unit $\langle\vec\sigma\rangle$ forces an eigenvector of $\vec e\cdot\vec\sigma$ with eigenvalue $+1$

encounters.title: Spin-1/2 prepared along $\vec n$, measured along $z$ (sheet 11 Q2, FS24 Q3(b))
encounters.problem: A spin-1/2 is in the state with $\langle\vec\sigma\rangle=\vec n=(\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta)$. $S_z$ is measured. Find $P(S_z=+\hbar/2)$, $\langle S_z\rangle$ and $\Delta S_z$. Source: sheet 11 Q2; FS24 Q3(b).
symbols: polar angle of $\vec n$ from the $z$ axis

derivation.title: Method
derivation.html: The state is the $+1$ eigenvector of $\vec n\cdot\vec\sigma$; its components in the $S_z$ basis give the probabilities; $\langle S_z\rangle=\frac\hbar2(P_+-P_-)$ and $\Delta S_z^2=\frac{\hbar^2}4-\langle S_z\rangle^2$ because $S_z^2=\hbar^2/4$.

why.0: Spinors carry half angles; $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ would give $\langle\sigma_3\rangle=\cos2\theta$.
why.2: This has $\langle\sigma_3\rangle=-\cos\theta$: spin along $-\vec n$ reflected.
why.3: Rotation about $z$ only changes the phase of the spinor; $\vec n$ has to come from a rotation about $y$.

steps.prompt: Bonus: $\Delta S_z$ for $\theta=60^\circ$ in units of $\hbar$.

derivation.html: Selection rule for the means, the commutator trick for $\langle L_1^2\rangle=\langle L_2^2\rangle$, the Casimir for the sum.

why.2: It is an eigenstate of $L_3$; $L_1$ has three different eigenvalues in $j=1$.
why.3: It holds for every $m$ by the ladder argument.

Sum rule $\vec L^2-L_3^2=\hbar^2[l(l+1)-m^2]$, split equally between $L_1^2$ and $L_2^2$.

encounters.problem: The 3D oscillator $V=\frac12m\omega^2\vec x^2$ has the eigenfunctions $\psi_i=x_ie^{-m\omega\vec x^2/2\hbar}$. Show that $[H,L_j]=0$, find the energy of the $\psi_i$ and the eigenvectors of $L_3$ in their span. Source: FS26 Q3.

derivation.title: Method
derivation.html: Symmetry from $\vec x\wedge\nabla V=0$; energy from the $N=1$ level; $L_3\psi_k=-i\hbar\varepsilon_{3ak}\psi_a$, a $3\times3$ matrix with eigenvectors $\psi_1\pm i\psi_2$, $\psi_3$.

options: Because the potential is harmonic and $[H,x_j]=0$
$\nabla V=m\omega^2\vec x$ is parallel to $\vec x$, so $\varepsilon_{jkl}x_k\partial_lV=m\omega^2\varepsilon_{jkl}x_kx_l=0$

why.0: $x_j$ does not commute with the kinetic term; the symmetry is rotational, not translational.
why.1: This is irrelevant; the antisymmetry of $\varepsilon$ does the work.
why.2: Even potentials need not be rotation invariant.

steps.hint: $\psi_i$ is the first excited level of the 3D oscillator, $E=\hbar\omega(N+\frac32)$ with $N=1$.

encounters.title: Angular momentum, measurements, and uncertainty (FS26 Q1)

source.where: Question 1 [Angular momentum, measurements, and uncertainty, 20 points]

encounters.instructions: Solve all parts on paper under the timer (2 min per point). Then enter the final numbers; the derivations are graded by you against the key points.
statement: (i) With $L_j=\varepsilon_{jkl}x_kp_l$ show $[L_j,L_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}L_l$ (hint: $[L_1,L_2]=i\hbar L_3$ and cyclicity). [5 pt]
The spin-$j$ representation is spanned by $|j,m\rangle$ with $L_3|j,m\rangle=\hbar m|j,m\rangle$ and $L_\pm|j,m\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m\pm1)}\,|j,m\pm1\rangle$.
(ii) $j=1$, unknown state, $L_1$ measured with result $\hbar$. Show that afterwards $|\psi\rangle=\frac12(|1,1\rangle+\sqrt2|1,0\rangle+|1,-1\rangle)$. [3 pt]
(iii) Measure $L_3$ in $|\psi\rangle$: outcomes, probabilities and $\langle L_3\rangle$. [3 pt]
(iv) Show $0=\langle\psi|[L_1,O]|\psi\rangle$ for any $O$ and use it to show $\langle L_2\rangle=0$ and $\langle L_2^2\rangle=\langle L_3^2\rangle$. [4 pt]
(v) Compute the uncertainties $\Delta L_j$ and show that the Heisenberg uncertainty principle holds for all $\Delta L_j\Delta L_k$ (hint: $\Delta L_2=\Delta L_3$). [5 pt]
keyPoints: (ii) eigenvector of $L_1=\frac\hbar{\sqrt2}(\ldots)$ with eigenvalue $\hbar$: $b=\sqrt2a$, $a=c$; normalisation gives $\frac12(1,\sqrt2,1)$
(iv) $\langle L_1O-OL_1\rangle=\hbar\langle O\rangle-\hbar\langle O\rangle=0$; $O=L_3$ gives $\langle L_2\rangle=0$; $O=L_2L_3+L_3L_2$ gives $\langle L_2^2\rangle=\langle L_3^2\rangle$
(v) $\langle L_1^2\rangle=\hbar^2$, $\vec L^2=2\hbar^2$ so $\langle L_2^2\rangle=\langle L_3^2\rangle=\frac{\hbar^2}2$; $\Delta L_1=0$, $\Delta L_{2,3}=\hbar/\sqrt2$
(v) bound: $\Delta L_2\Delta L_3=\frac{\hbar^2}2=\frac\hbar2|\langle L_1\rangle|$ saturated; the other products are $0\ge0$

encounters.title: Angular momentum (FS22 Q2)
encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer (2 min per point), then enter the numbers for $l=3$, $m=2$.
statement: The angular momentum operator is defined by $L_j=-i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}x_k\partial_{x_l}$, $j=1,2,3$.
(i) Show $[L_j,L_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}L_l$ (hint: work out $[L_1,L_2]$ and argue by symmetry). [2 pt]
(ii) With $L_\pm=L_1\pm iL_2$ compute $[L_3,L_\pm]$ and $[L_+,L_-]$ in terms of these generators. [2 pt]
(iii) In an irreducible representation $L_3|l,m\rangle=\hbar m|l,m\rangle$, $L_\pm|l,m\rangle=\hbar\sqrt{l(l+1)-m(m\pm1)}|l,m\pm1\rangle$. Show $\langle L_1\rangle=\langle L_2\rangle=0$. [3 pt]
(iv) Determine $\Delta L_1$, $\Delta L_2$ and show $\Delta L_1\Delta L_2=\frac12\hbar^2[l(l+1)-m^2]$. [5 pt]
(v) State the Heisenberg relation for $L_1,L_2$, compute the lower bound and show that (7) is compatible. [3 pt]

finalAnswers.prompt: $\Delta L_1\Delta L_2$ for $l=3$, $m=2$ in units of $\hbar^2$.
The lower bound $\frac12|\langle[L_1,L_2]\rangle|$ for $l=3$, $m=2$ in units of $\hbar^2$.
The product $\Delta L_1\Delta L_2$ for $l=m=2$ in units of $\hbar^2$ (equality case).

keyPoints: (i) $[L_1,L_2]=i\hbar L_3$ from conjugate pairs; cyclicity/antisymmetry for the rest
(iii) $L_{1,2}$ are combinations of $L_\pm$, which map to $m\pm1\perp m$
(v) $\Delta L_1\Delta L_2\ge\frac\hbar2|\langle L_3\rangle|=\frac{\hbar^2|m|}2$; $l(l+1)-m^2\ge l\ge|m|$, equality for $|m|=l$

encounters.title: Rotational symmetry (FS26 Q3)
encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer (2 min per point), then enter the numbers.
statement: (i) Show $[H,L_j]\psi=0$ for any $\psi$ iff $\varepsilon_{jkl}x_k\frac{\partial V}{\partial x_l}=0$ (hint: first show $[\nabla^2,x_k\partial_l]\psi=2\partial_k\partial_l\psi$). [5 pt]
(ii) Show that for $V=V(r)$ the Hamiltonian is rotationally symmetric. What does this imply for the eigenstates and the degeneracies? [4 pt]
(iii) Show that $\psi_i=x_ie^{-m\omega\vec x^2/2\hbar}$ are eigenfunctions of $H$. What are the energies? [5 pt]
(iv) Show that $L_j\psi_k\in\mathrm{span}\{\psi_1,\psi_2,\psi_3\}$ and find the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of $L_3$ in this space. [5 pt]

finalAnswers.prompt: Energy of the $\psi_i$ in units of $\hbar\omega$.
Degeneracy of this level from rotational symmetry ($\ell=1$).
Eigenvalue of $L_3$ on $\psi_1+i\psi_2$ in units of $\hbar$.
Eigenvalue of $L_3$ on $\psi_3$ in units of $\hbar$.

keyPoints: (i) $[\nabla^2,x_k\partial_l]=2\partial_k\partial_l$ is symmetric in $k,l$ and vanishes against $\varepsilon_{jkl}$; $[V,L_j]\psi=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}x_k(\partial_lV)\psi$
